catalog_locator: p. 358 (general pattern, ex. 32) and p. 367 (Conclusion) — both checked against the rendered page image (PDF pp. 18, 27); heavy-syllable definition p. 349; all-light words pp. 355-356; exceptions pp. 358-359; abstract pp. 341-342 (text layer)
catalog_quote: As can be seen in Table 6, two-syllable words with two heavy syllables normally have primary stress on the final syllable. Longer words with multiple heavy syllables usually have primary stress on the rightmost heavy syllable that is not word-final (32). Note that this pattern is different from what Piggott (1980) says about Odawa. In that dialect, primary stress falls on the penultimate stressed vowel of a word with only two stressed vowels and on the antepenultimate stressed vowel of a word with three or more stressed vowels. So basically in Border Lakes Ojibwe primary stress is one stressed syllable to the right of where it falls in Odawa. [p. 358] ... Conclusions about stress in Border Lakes Ojibwe are as follows. – Feet are iambs, assigned from left to right. – Degenerate feet are not allowed. – There is a layer of binary right-headed cola; the prosodic word is also right-headed. – Perceived primary stress correlates with the longest vowel. – Primary stress falls on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable except in cases (such as HH') in which the construction of a colon forces it onto the final heavy syllable. [p. 367] ... heavy syllables are stressed. ... Generally, words with four or more light syllables (21a-c) are stressed on every second syllable starting from the left although there are some words in which the initial syllable is stressed (21b). [p. 355]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., text layer; extracted text page 18 = printed p. 358, page 27 = printed p. 367) and the companion (lines 652-676 and 1050-1082). The p. 358 passage is there verbatim apart from scanned letter-spacing artifacts ("O d a w a", "o n" for "on"): "As can be seen in Table 6, two-syllable words with two heavy syllables normally have primary stress on the final syllable. Longer words with multiple heavy syllables usually have primary stress on the rightmost heavy syllable that is not word-final (32). Note that this pattern is different from what Piggott (1980) says about Odawa. In that dialect, primary stress falls on the penultimate stressed vowel of a word with only two stressed vow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iambic feet are built from the left edge; a syllable with a long vowel (heavy) is always stressed and forms its own foot head; in strings of light syllables every second syllable from the left is stressed (LL, LLL, LLLL.. -> 2nd, 2nd, 2nd+4th). Primary stress goes to the rightmost heavy syllable that is not word-final; in two-syllable heavy-heavy words it falls on the final syllable; in words with a single initial heavy syllable that syllable carries primary stress. Vowel duration is the phonetic cue; pitch is not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Every other foot head carries secondary stress: 'the heavy syllable has primary stress and every second syllable starting from the heavy syllable has secondary stress' (p. 357, ex. 25, e.g. zhaabonigaanan 'needles'); in some 4-syllable HLLL words the final syllable takes secondary stress instead (ex. 26); with six light syllables the primary/secondary split between 2nd and 4th syllable could not be determined.
new_statements.exceptions: HH disyllables stress the final syllable (11 of 14; 3 initial, e.g. miigwech, oojiins, gookoosh); words whose expected stressed vowel is /e:/ vary (miigwech, memengwaa); suffixes with long vowels (plural -n, 3pl -g, diminutive -ns) usually attract primary stress (baashka'amoog, waagaakwadoon, enigoons) but not always (mitigwaabiin); some LLL words stress the final syllable (particle ningoding; -ad finals dibikad, mizhakwad, giizhigad) and one the initial (ogitig); obligatorily possessed otawag final in sg; six-light-syllable words: 2nd vs 4th syllable indistinguishable; 4-syllable HLLL words alternate between H-primary-with-alternating-secondary and H-primary-with-final-secondary.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 185 nouns, verbs and particles (mainly citation forms) elicited in isolation, in the carrier sentence miinawaa ___ nindikid, and hummed; measurements from the carrier-sentence tokens; two consultants from Chima'aganing (Seine River) Reserve, Ontario; primary stress = perceived stress checked against vowel duration.
new_statements.identity_note: The first-hand statement (Swierzbin 2003) describes Border Lakes Ojibwe, spoken by two consultants from Chima'aganing (Seine River) Reserve, Ontario, near the Minnesota border — i.e. Glottolog's dialect Minnesota Border Chippewa [minn1250] under chip1241; Swierzbin states it is 'quite similar' to Chippewa (Minnesota Ojibwe) and checks forms against Nichols & Nyholm 1995. Her primary-stress rule (rightmost non-final heavy syllable) is explicitly one stressed syllable to the right of the Odawa antepenultimate rule (Piggott 1980), and differs from the secondary-source 'antepenultimate foot' rule circulating for Minnesota/SW Ojibwe (Wikipedia/native-languages.org, citing Valentine 2001 = Nishnaabemwin); the central Mille Lacs variety has no accessible first-hand statement (Nichols 1980; Nichols & Nyholm 1995 not open).

sources.note: Acoustic study (185 words, 2 speakers, Seine River/Chima'aganing, Ontario): duration is the stress correlate; iambic feet L-to-R, no degenerate feet, heavy (long-vowel) syllables stressed; primary stress on the rightmost NON-final heavy syllable (HH disyllables: final); all-light words stressed on every second syllable from the left; explicitly differs from Odawa (Piggott 1980) by one stressed syllable to the right.
